title: Eco Village Malo Buchino
location: Malo Buchino, Ovcha Kupel District, Sofia Municipality, Bulgaria
developedWith: Independent master’s thesis projectSupervisor: Prof. Dr. Arch. Georgiev
shortDescription: A master’s thesis project for an eco-oriented residential village in Malo Buchino, combining low-rise housing, public services, green infrastructure, renewable energy systems, and shared community spaces into a model for sustainable suburban living.
overview: Eco Village Malo Buchino is a large-scale residential project located in the Sofia Municipality, within Ovcha Kupel District. The project proposes a low-rise settlement with detached houses, row houses, multifamily buildings, and a public-service centre, all organized as one ecological community rather than a conventional suburban development.
concept: The project asks whether a residential neighbourhood can function as a more responsible model of suburban living. Instead of treating housing as isolated private plots, the design combines homes, public services, green spaces, pedestrian routes, shared gardens, and sustainable systems into one connected settlement structure.
functions: The programme includes 89 detached single-family houses, 40 row houses, 8 three-storey multifamily residential buildings, and a public-service centre. The centre includes a kindergarten, restaurant, spa and fitness centre, supermarket, medical office, pharmacy, multifunctional halls, community spaces, a central park, a square, gardens, and a chapel.
architecturalSolution: The urban structure is based on low-rise residential development with free-standing and complex housing arrangements. Buildings are organized around pedestrian-friendly green spaces, with reduced internal car traffic, cycling routes, shared infrastructure, and a central public zone that gives the settlement a clear community focus.
sustainabilityFocus: The project integrates passive house principles, photovoltaic panels, geothermal systems, ventilation with heat recovery, greywater and rainwater reuse, composting, green roofs, local vegetation, biodiversity zones, and electric mobility. Sustainability is treated as a full settlement strategy, not only as a technical feature of the individual buildings.
reflection: This project is important in my portfolio because it brings together architecture, urban planning, ecology, infrastructure, and everyday life at a larger scale. It helped me understand how sustainable architecture can move beyond the single building and become a system of housing, mobility, energy, water, food, public space, and community.

title: Residential Building in Manastirski Livadi
developedWith: In collaboration with a colleague architect
shortDescription: A higher-end multifamily residential building in Manastirski Livadi, Sofia, combining spacious apartments, ground-floor homes with private yards, garages, underground parking, and the potential for green roof areas.
overview: The project is a multifamily residential building located in Manastirski Livadi, one of Sofia’s rapidly developing residential districts. It explores a more spacious and refined model of urban apartment living, where comfort, functional clarity, and access to outdoor space become central parts of the design.
concept: The project asks how an apartment building can offer a stronger sense of home within a dense urban context. Instead of focusing only on compact units, the design gives more attention to larger apartments, private yard spaces, parking organization, and the possibility of integrating green roof areas.
functions: The building includes underground parking, garages and parking spaces on the ground level, ground-floor apartments with private yards, and typical residential floors above. The apartment layouts are developed with more generous spatial organization, supporting a higher level of comfort and everyday functionality.
architecturalSolution: The architectural solution is based on a clear residential structure that balances living areas, parking, access, and outdoor spaces. The ground-floor apartments with private yards create a softer transition between the building and its site, while the upper levels continue the residential programme through larger apartment types.
sustainabilityFocus: The sustainable potential of the project is connected to green roof areas, private yards, underground parking, and a more efficient organization of the urban plot. These elements support better use of available space while creating additional outdoor areas within a dense residential district.
reflection: This project is important in my portfolio because it shows my experience with a higher-end professional residential building and the detailed logic behind apartment planning. It helped me work with the balance between comfort, market expectations, parking requirements, outdoor space, and the practical constraints of urban housing.

title: Residential Building in Obelya
developedWith: In collaboration with a colleague architect
shortDescription: A mixed-use residential building in Obelya, Sofia, combining housing with public services, a gallery-access system, and an internal peristyle courtyard that strengthens the building’s social and spatial identity.
overview: The project is a professional residential building in Obelya with a dominant housing function and additional public services. It combines apartments with a children’s centre, grocery store, beauty studio, and medical centre, creating a building that serves both its residents and the surrounding neighbourhood.
concept: The project asks how a residential building can become more than a collection of apartments. By combining housing with everyday services and organizing the residential levels around an internal courtyard, the design explores a more active and community-oriented model of urban living.
functions: The programme includes residential units, a children’s centre, grocery store, beauty studio, medical centre, shared circulation spaces, and an internal courtyard. The public functions support daily needs, while the gallery-access residential levels create a more open relationship between private apartments and shared space.
architecturalSolution: The architectural solution is defined by the gallery-access system and the internal peristyle courtyard. This organization turns circulation into more than a technical corridor; it becomes part of the spatial identity of the building and creates visual and social connections between the different levels.
sustainabilityFocus: The sustainable value of the project is connected to mixed use, compact urban living, natural light, and the social potential of the internal courtyard. By integrating everyday services within the building, the project supports a more walkable neighbourhood logic and reduces the need for separate trips for basic functions.
reflection: This project is important in my portfolio because it shows my professional experience with a more complex residential typology. It helped me explore how housing can support not only private living, but also shared space, daily convenience, and a stronger relationship between the building and its urban context.

title: Townhouse Residential Complex, Bistritsa
developedWith: In collaboration with a colleague architect
shortDescription: A compact townhouse residential complex in Bistritsa, designed as a functional suburban housing model with southern exposure, large terraces, flexible upper-level spaces, and efficient family-oriented layouts.
overview: The project proposes a complex of row houses in Bistritsa, a suburban area of Sofia known for low-rise residential development and proximity to natural landscapes. It was designed as a more accessible model of family housing, where compact volumes still preserve the feeling of a private home.
concept: The project asks how a budget-conscious townhouse can remain functional, comfortable, and spatially generous. Instead of treating compactness as a limitation, the design uses it as a framework for clear layouts, flexible upper-level spaces, and strong connections to outdoor terraces.
functions: Each townhouse is developed for family living, with a clear residential programme, three bedrooms, and the possibility for an additional small studio or flexible space on the upper level. Large terraces and southern exposure strengthen the relationship between the interior spaces and the surrounding suburban landscape.
architecturalSolution: The architectural solution is based on compact row-house volumes that use the plot efficiently while respecting the low-rise character of Bistritsa. The design focuses on practical layouts, clear circulation, good orientation, and exterior spaces that make the houses feel more open than their compact footprint suggests.
sustainabilityFocus: The sustainable value of the project is connected to land efficiency, compact housing, southern exposure, and the rational use of space. As a row-house structure, the project offers a more efficient alternative to fully detached suburban houses while still preserving key qualities of family living, such as individual entrances, terraces, and a direct connection to the outdoor environment.
reflection: This project is important in my portfolio because it shows my experience with real residential design under practical spatial and market constraints. It helped me work with the balance between budget, comfort, compactness, and architectural quality — a balance that is essential in professional housing projects.

title: Research and Innovation Complex, Sofia Tech Park
shortDescription: A low-rise research and innovation complex in Sofia Tech Park, designed as a connected mat-building system where laboratories, offices, public services, residential areas, terraces, and green roofs form a compact urban ecosystem for work, research, and everyday life.
overview: This project explores how a research complex can become more than an institutional workplace. Located in Sofia Tech Park, it brings together laboratories, offices, public services, residential areas, recreation, and green roof spaces into one integrated architectural system.
concept: The design is based on the idea of a decentralized urban centre - a smaller self-sufficient community within the larger city. Instead of separating work, living, services, and leisure, the project allows these functions to overlap within a connected research campus.
functions: The complex includes research laboratories, offices, an auditorium, seminar spaces, a restaurant, a shop, fitness and spa areas, residential zones, terraces, and underground parking. Public and service-oriented functions are placed on the lower levels, while laboratories, offices, workspaces, and terraces develop through the upper floors.
architecturalSolution: The architectural solution uses a mat-building approach, spreading the programme through connected low-rise volumes instead of concentrating it in a single vertical tower. This creates a continuous spatial system where movement, work, services, public areas, and green spaces are closely connected.
sustainabilityFocus: Sustainability is developed through green roofs, internal green areas, natural light, recyclable material strategies, and the relationship between architecture and landscape. The green roof system supports thermal performance, rainwater management, and a softer working environment within a highly specialized research programme.
reflection: This project helped me understand how a complex programme can gain strength through connection rather than monumentality. It became an early step in my interest in architecture as social and ecological infrastructure - a way to support work, movement, wellbeing, and community within one built system.

title: Single-family House by the Seaside
shortDescription: A minimalist single-family house near Tsarevo, designed for year-round living with a strong focus on sea views, eastern exposure, clear volumetric composition, and restrained material expression.
overview: This project explores how a seaside house can function as a permanent home rather than a seasonal vacation object. The design provides a full residential programme for a family, while keeping the architectural language simple, controlled, and oriented toward the view.
concept: The concept is based on achieving a strong architectural presence through a very simple composition of two volumes. Inspired by the early Bauhaus understanding of clarity and functional form, the project develops this logic in a softer residential context, where the sea view, light, and horizon become part of the design.
functions: The house includes a living area with kitchenette, garage, office, foyer, bathrooms, three bedrooms, wardrobe spaces, and a usable roof terrace. The basement level contains a fitness area, sauna, laundry, shower, storage spaces, technical rooms, and pool filtration spaces, supporting the house as a complete year-round residence.
architecturalSolution: The architectural solution relies on clean geometry, horizontal emphasis, and large glazed openings facing the landscape. The two-volume composition creates a clear silhouette without unnecessary decoration, allowing the building to feel both minimal and expressive.
sustainabilityFocus: The sustainable approach is connected to material restraint, passive use of natural light, orientation toward the eastern exposure, and the possibility of using recyclable timber-based elements and recycled cladding materials. The project treats minimalism not as an aesthetic shortcut, but as a way to reduce visual and material excess while strengthening the relationship with the site.
reflection: This project is important in my portfolio because it shows how a simple form can still create a memorable architectural image. It helped me understand that architectural strength does not always come from complexity; sometimes it comes from proportion, orientation, material clarity, and the discipline to let the context become the main focus.
